# Recommendations for Eric Rash

Private planning document. Built from the four module notes, `notes/eric-context.md`, and the 2026-07-29 all-staff meeting transcript (Fireflies, unverified auto-transcript; only structural content is used here). Where a staff characterization is an inference from the brief rather than a stated fact, it is marked (inferred). No athlete names or health information appear.

Tags on each recommendation:

- **now**: pays off this semester whether or not anyone else adopts it.
- **outlives**: only pays off if it is still running after mid-2027 without you.
- **portfolio**: produces evidence of department-building you could show in an interview. Never the point, always a by-product.

## 1. What the course assumes and you do not have

The course is written for a high-performance manager who owns the physios and the strength coaches, sits with the head coach, and can say "this is how we will proceed" (module-2 note, Stacking_Evidence p.3). You own neither side of the grey zone. Applied Performance is a support function behind Athletic Medicine and Athletic Performance, you report to the Director of Athletic Performance, you have no budget line, and the July JD left authority thresholds undefined. Most of Module 4 (phase ownership, one operational logic, communication protocol) needs a sponsor who owns the clinical to training interface. That sponsor now exists: the late-July restructure named a Senior Associate AD for Athlete Health and a new Athletics Healthcare Advisory Group (section 3).

So the rule for every recommendation below: **install on ground you own, offer on ground others own.** Ground you own: the Applied Performance staff meeting, the 1:1s with AJ and Noah, the biweekly status report, Research in 5, the project charters, the intern and SOP templates, the tech inventory, your own PD folder. Ground others own: care teams, return-to-play gates, the Athletic Performance staff meeting, the software approval path. Your August blowback for acting unasked on claimed ground is the boundary; the course's "this is how we will proceed" only works on unclaimed ground.

## 2. Where the course collides with your current approach

Sharpened, as asked.

1. **Your summer scorecard is the course's thesis.** Everything that needed you to start and finish a document scored near zero (0.23 average). The two things that scored 1.0 were adopted practices: dashboards in weekly use and the AJ handoff. The course says the same thing from the other direction: "a device doesn't create impact, a workflow does" (Lab_2b p.1). Stop counting documents as output. Count adoption signals (a second person uses it, a coach declines to react to noise, a meeting ends with a logged decision).

2. **Four education decks on the Fall slate repeats the pattern that failed twice.** Education is 0-for-3 for two cycles. The July reset (advance notice, email now, website later) fixed the launch loop but not the medium: decks nobody asked for, pushed to a mixed audience. The course's cheaper route is Lab 3D: education happens inside meetings you already run, one topic, one slide, one time box, then a debrief (Lab_3D_Blog pp.1-2). Cut the KR to two pieces at the Oct 15 checkpoint unless one of the first two has a documented adoption signal.

3. **The Education Alignment Initiative is over-scoped against the course.** Forty-five topics, eight domains, a Performance School and a Performance Academy, an Education Czar proposal. Lab 3D's whole method is "simple meeting, one topic, one slide, one time box, debrief, repeat" (Lab_3D_Blog p.2). The initiative has produced three decks and thirteen documents. Pause it. Keep the deck design system as a tool.

4. **HPI as "standardized underneath, bespoke on top" risks building infrastructure before the question.** Lab 2C's warning is technology-led practice: "we have force plates, so we should jump" (Lab_2c p.2). The means-first version of HPI already exists in the course: the Capability and Workflow Matrix (Lab_2b pp.2-3). HPI v1 should be one filled column of that matrix for one sport, with owners and a workflow, not a data platform. If a platform is still needed after the column is filled, the column is the requirements document.

5. **The tech inventory for Kenny is not the Lab 1C audit.** It is a software-by-unit inventory (188 products, 32 units). The Lab 1C Tech Stack Reality Check is a measurement-system audit of your own devices: raw signal, derived metric, reliability source, one one-page procedure (Lab_1c p.4). Do not conflate them and do not let the second get absorbed by the first. The honest first row of the 1C audit is "we don't know yet" for most VALD and Catapult metrics in your environment, and that is the work list, not an embarrassment.

6. **You review every artifact before it leaves the department.** That is the "Oversee" definition for AJ. The course calls this where leaders lose control of time (module-3 note, Webinar 3 Part III, transcript-only) and prescribes scaled lanes: a first-year hire gets one or two, a trusted colleague gets all six. AJ's fall-camp handoff scored 1.0. Widen his lanes in writing by Spring.

7. **The care-team reform is a meeting-typology change happening without the vocabulary.** The AD said sport administrators will lead sport care teams, that composition is set by the support units, and that a care team with extra people "is just a staff meeting" (all-staff 2026-07-29, approx 01:26 to 01:47, unverified transcript). That is Lab 3B's "one meeting, one primary job" argument. The play is to offer the typology cheat sheet to one sport administrator through Chris, not to install it.

8. **No AMS platform decision is pending.** Kitman stays. (Correction 2026-09-24: earlier notes described a "Kitman vs MyLink" decision. That was an error. The vendor is Myelin, a startup AMS Baylor will not do business with. There is no platform comparison.) The course question still applies to Kitman itself: which cell of the Capability and Workflow Matrix does each Kitman feature you use actually fill (Lab_2b pp.2-3)?

9. **Program_Context_Meet was designed in July and has not run.** It is the Lab 2C five coach questions in reverse (what are we evaluating, why, how often, what do you receive, what do we do if it changes; Lab_2c p.2). Run two of them, not all, and fold the five questions in.

## 3. What changed in late July

From the 2026-07-29 all-staff meeting (about two hours; Fireflies transcript, unverified). Structural content only.

- Carrie (transcript renders "Kerry"; same person, inferred) was promoted to Senior Associate AD of Athlete Health, leading mental health services and athletic health integration (approx 00:56).
- The AD listed the standalone units of equal importance: Athletic Medicine, mental health services, Performance Nutrition, Athletic Performance, academic services, student-athlete formation (approx 00:57). Applied Performance was not in that list. Inference: this is a visibility signal, not a slight; the unit is seen through Athletic Performance. It is also the strongest argument for shipped proof over persuasion.
- Two new roles: an Ethics Case Manager (onboarding, screening, intake, support; meant to serve multiple units) and an NIL Education role (approx 01:00 to 01:03).
- Sport Care Team reform: sport administrators lead; composition is set by the support areas, not coaches; explicitly distinguished from a staff meeting; confidentiality guidelines apply (approx 01:26 to 01:47). The Clinical Care Team is licensed providers only, confidential under state law, and doubles as the crisis response team (approx 01:28 to 01:30).
- Athletics Healthcare Advisory Group is new, with an audit and review-of-significant-events purpose; Carrie and senior Athletic Medicine staff build it out (approx 01:36 to 01:37).
- Teamworks utilization will be enforced from the AD's level with compliance involved; the software and technology approval process now involves general counsel and ITS (Jon Allen) with the aim of a streamlined approval path (approx 01:39, 01:48).
- Requirements on all staff: personal PD folders by Sept 30; annual unit reporting with data collected by September for strategy and resource requests; weekly 11:15 to 11:45 check-ins; documentation as a requirement, not a suggestion (approx 01:06, 01:16, 01:20, 02:02).

What this means for the plan: the sponsor for Module 4 work is Carrie via the advisory group; the Sport Care Team is now a sport administrator's forum, not yours; the software approval question that blocked the tech framework has moved to general counsel and ITS, which makes the standing ITS meeting more useful, not less; and the unit report Doug asked for is the visibility vehicle you were trying to create with the briefing asset.

## 4. Recommendations mapped onto vehicles you already control

| Biweekly status report to Chris and Kenny | Keep five headings and 300 words. Write every Decisions Needed line in stoplight form: status, one ask as a verb, owner, review date. Where a number is cited, add its error band once you have it. Report #3 is owed; do not count it as new work. | Lab_3c template p.1; cheat sheet p.1 | now, portfolio |
| Fall 2026 slate and project charters | Each charter's "plan agreed with receiver" step becomes a Kaigi: two or three options in a pre-read email, a date, a logged answer. Add a "decision gate" line to each charter: what result at the mid-point means continue, reshape or stop. | Lab_3a pp.1-2; Lab_2D p.1 | now |
| OKR gate decision (AI integration, data governance) | Treat as a Kaigi with yourself as arbiter. Park AI integration (policy-restricted, pilot done). Data governance folds into the NCAA best-practices doc only if Anthony's proposal arrives by Oct 15; otherwise park. Log both with a review date. | Lab_3a p.1 | now |
| Oct 15 mid-semester checkpoint | Run it as an After Action Review on the slate: facts, what could not be measured, procedure changes, owners. Cut the education KR here if no adoption signal. | Cheat sheet p.2; Lab_3b_Blog p.2 | now |
| Applied Performance staff meeting (announced, biweekly) | Make it exist. Invite carries modality, objective, duration, prep. Segment: Inform 10 min, Diagnose 15 min, Decide 5 min, named out loud. Decision log in a Teams channel, kept by a rotating "on audit" person (AJ first cycle, Noah second). This is where Lab 3D reps happen. | Cheat sheet pp.1-2; Lab_3a p.2; Lab_3D worksheet | outlives, portfolio |
| Weekly 1:1 with AJ | Ops stand-up form: what happened, what is blocked, who owns it, what is next. Log micro-decisions. Use it to write the football empowerment checklist (section 5). | Cheat sheet p.2; Grey Zone Workbook p.6 | now, outlives |
| Biweekly 1:1 with Noah | The Lab 3D ladder lives here: pick the rep, set guardrails, debrief after. | Lab_3D_Worksheet pp.1-3 | outlives |
| Your PD folder (due Sept 30) | The K-B self-audit (Workbook B1 to B3 and D1) is the content. It answers Doug's ask and the course's first exercise in one move. | Student Workbook pp.2-4 | now |
| Tech inventory for Kenny (due 10-09) | Ship as scoped. In the findings, apply one course filter to the retention question for the 123 single-unit products: is the product in any workflow that ends in a decision? If not, it is a candidate for retirement. Report-out to Cody, Jovon and Kenny as three bullets: decisions, actions, review date. The July 29 change (general counsel and ITS own approval) is the reason to re-send the request. | Cheat sheet p.2; Lab_3D worksheet Part B | now |
| Research in 5 | Decide the pending readout question yes: the three-slide readout is the stoplight format (question, status, one chart, one ask, owner, review). Lead with the recommendation in the first 20 seconds. Measure by replies and uses, not sends. | Lab_3c pp.1-2; module-4 note 6D transcript-only | now, portfolio |
| RTP constraints course (receiver Joe Smith) | Add two course pieces as lesson content: the measured / inferred / probability / next step report form, and a one-page decision gate exercise Joe writes for his own session. Keep the six-lesson scope. | Lab_2a pp.3-4; Lab_2D pp.1-2 | now, outlives |

## 5. Per-person staff development

Course logic used: place each person on the two axes with evidence, choose the single axis to move this semester, give reps not advice, scale lanes to experience (Grey Zone Workbook pp.2-3, 6; Lab_3D worksheet). Placements are inferences from the brief and should be checked against your own observation and, where the course recommends it, with Chris. Whether you have input on AJ's and Noah's reviews is still an open question to Chris; everything below is doable under "oversee" and "support and guide".

### AJ Tademy, Applied Performance Specialist, Football

Evidence: fall-camp handoff scored 1.0; owns the practice-load framework and the plan-vs-actual review; jointly presented the framework to football staff before the handoff; runs football communications. No gap stated in any source.

Placement (inferred): Practitioner on knowledge, approaching Operator inside the football load domain; Catalyst on behaviour. The course says anchor your protocols on the catalyst (Grey Zone Workbook p.3). He is also, on the evidence, the succession candidate for the football lane and possibly the unit. Say so to him and to Chris before Spring, because the "outlives" recommendations in this document depend on it.

Delegate:

- The "on audit" decision-log role for the first staff-meeting cycle (module-3 note, Lab 3A, transcript-only). It is the cheapest visible responsibility and it teaches the log.
- The football Decision Empowerment Checklist, adapted to a non-athlete-facing role. Write the seven rows with him in a 1:1: change a threshold in the practice-load model; send a report to football staff without your review; respond to an ad hoc coach request with a new cut of data; add a variable mid-season (the course says never; Webinar 3, transcript-only); change the day-colour classification; escalate a load concern to Athletic Medicine; escalate to you. Mark which rows he already exercises de facto (most of the first three, inferred) and which are unwritten. The unwritten rows are the lanes you widen in Spring.

Reps:

- Run one Diagnose segment of the staff meeting on a problem he names.

Watch for: single-signal calls under coach pressure on game week (the course's evidence-stack rule); territorial bias, which is the Operator check (Grey Zone Workbook p.2); and your own reflex to review everything, which is the real constraint on his growth. Tag: now, outlives.

### Noah, Basketball Applied Performance GA

Evidence: "training wheels on"; you teach procedures and data-management practice; summer onboarding KR scored 0.0. That score is evidence about your onboarding, not about Noah, and should be read that way. Basketball is self-contained and resistant, so adoption is not a fair measure of him. Position after the GA term is an open question to Chris.

Placement (inferred, low confidence): Pawn on knowledge, which the course defines as "can execute clearly defined tasks and build momentum" and which is the right place for a GA (Lab_1b p.2). No behaviour evidence either way.

Delegate: nothing that requires him to win basketball's cooperation. Give him tasks whose completion is inside his control.

Reps (Lab 3D ladder, low stakes first, step-up rule four of five criteria):

1. Rep 1, October: run the 10-minute ops stand-up segment of the staff meeting. Guardrails: name the modality, three questions, end on time. Debrief five minutes after.
2. Rep 2, November: one stoplight slide on one basketball metric with SEM and MDC95 stated, even if the values are vendor-published with the caveat written on the slide.
3. Rep 3, November or December: one one-page procedure for one device he runs (Lab_1c p.3). This is the artifact that survives if his position ends.
4. Rep 4, December: keep the decision log for one cycle.

Watch for: hesitation at transitions, which the course names as the Pawn pattern and treats as a supervision problem, not a talent problem (Grey Zone Workbook p.2); and Pawn behaviour in a Practitioner role, holding back waiting for permission never withheld (Grey Zone Summary p.5). Tell him explicitly which decisions are his. Tag: outlives.

### Linda

Evidence: role under Applied Performance still being defined; leadership stated your role is supportive, not directive; two August meetings produced four candidate projects for Tennis and Athletic Performance. No knowledge or behaviour evidence in any source.

Placement: none. Do not place her on the matrix on this evidence. Use the Lab 1B probes gently instead: ask what she is working on for CPD; invite one ten-minute presentation at the staff meeting on the project she cares most about.

Delegate: the means question. Of the four projects, which one has a receiver, a question, and a monitor-or-test answer (Lab_2c p.2)? Pick that one with her and drop the other three from the list until it ships. Four projects with no owner and no receiver is the pattern that ended your own earlier planning systems.

Watch for: the permission gate. Her role sits with Chris; anything directive is claimed ground. Tag: now.

### Student workers

Unnamed, uncounted in the sources. Give them the Lab 1C step 1 inventory (measurement-system tables for the devices they touch) and one procedure to follow exactly; procedure adherence is the check. Tag: outlives.

### You

Run the Student Workbook before you place anyone else. Your own answer to Option A or Option B (do you teach the framework, or empower the person who can) decides whether the education KR is yours at all (Module_6B_Part_B p.2). The brief says you know you under-educated colleagues on what the unit does; the course says constant re-explanation is diagnostic evidence, and the fix is education early, in the forums, not translation on demand.

| Athlete data governance | Hold to Oct 15, then park | Waiting on an external proposal since May. If it arrives, one section in the NCAA doc. | Gate with a timeframe (Lab_2D p.2) |
| Kitman (AMS) | Continue | No platform switch is under consideration; the Myelin comparison was an error in earlier notes. Map the Kitman features in use onto the matrix when HPI v1 is built. | Means first; Lab_2b matrix |
| White paper | Keep parked | Blake credited; no receiver pressure this semester. | Slate cap |
| Research repository MVP | Stop | Near zero twice; no receiver. | If not in a workflow it does not exist |
| Transformative_Athlete_Experience | Stop | No receiver, no date. | Same |
| Newsletter | Already stopped | Replaced by the education KR; do not revive. | Same |

## 7. Honest constraints

- **In-season.** AJ owns football operations. Nothing in the 30/60/90 touches football operations, football staff communications or the load model. The empowerment checklist is written about what already happens; it changes nothing on the field until Spring.
- **No budget, no protected time.** Every step below is under two hours except the Lab 2E reliability work, which is why that one has an honest "unknown with an off-season plan" fallback.
- **Baylor IT.** The decision log goes in Teams because Teams is the institutional surface that survives you. Not DEV, not the vault, not Drive.
- **Status-quo culture.** "If you're unhappy, go figure it out" is the environment. The course's response is procedures as the transparent way to find out who can work inside a collaborative system (Module_6B_Part_A p.2). You can only apply that inside your own unit.
- **Education 0-for-3, twice.** Named in section 2. The medium is the problem, not the launch.
- **Mid-2027 exit.** Items tagged "outlives" are worth doing only if AJ or a successor is named to carry them. If Chris will not have that conversation by December, downgrade every "outlives" item to "portfolio" and do only the cheap version.
- **Permission gate.** Section 1's rule. The care-team and advisory-group offers go through Chris in writing, once, and then wait.
- **Portfolio value, stated plainly.** The decision log, the matrix with a reliability column, the rep ladder with a debriefed junior, and the empowerment checklist are the four artifacts that show department-building rather than analysis. Each is also the right thing to do here. That is the whole reason to prefer them over another deck.

## 8. 30/60/90

Anchored to Oct 15 (checkpoint) and Dec 18 (semester close). Nothing here breaks in-season work.

### First week (by Oct 1). Three actions, under two hours total.

1. **K-B self-audit into your PD folder** (45 minutes). Workbook B1 to B3 and D1. It is due Sept 30 anyway. Tag: now.
2. **Rewrite two invites** (20 minutes). The next Applied Performance staff meeting and the next AJ 1:1: modality, objective, duration, required prep, on the invite itself. Create the Teams channel for the decision log and paste the CSV header from the stoplight template (Lab_3c template p.2). Tag: outlives.
3. **Send Kenny the overdue plan-agreed email for the tech inventory** (20 minutes). Two options for the deliverable shape, a date, one question. That is a Kaigi by email. Tag: now.

Also owed, not new work: status report #3, with the Decisions Needed lines in stoplight form.

### By day 30 (Oct 24)

- First staff meeting run with named segments and a log entry. AJ on audit. Noah rep 1 (ops stand-up segment).
- Oct 15 checkpoint run as an AAR: education KR cut to two unless an adoption signal exists; OKR gate logged (AI parked, governance held or parked).
- Tech inventory shipped 10-09 with the workflow filter applied to the retention question.
- Lab 1C submission for one device you run yourself (ForceDecks CMJ is the obvious one): inventory line, raw signal, derived metric, reliability source, one-page procedure into the Performance_Playbook SOP template. One page. Tag: outlives, portfolio.
- Program_Context_Meet run once (Volleyball), with the five coach questions.

### By day 60 (Nov 23)

- Capability and Workflow Matrix, one column for one sport, ten cells, owners named. This is HPI v1's scope; say so in the status report.
- Reliability table for the top five metrics, or "unknown" with a written off-season repeat-testing plan per row.
- AJ's first ten-minute presentation. Football empowerment checklist drafted with him in a 1:1, de facto rows marked.
- Noah rep 2 (stoplight slide with error band stated).
- Research in 5 issued in readout format; count replies.
- ITS stand-up running if Micah answers the re-sent request; three-bullet report-out to Cody, Jovon and Kenny after each.
- Annual unit report drafted from the briefing asset, submitted through Chris.

### By day 90 (Dec 18)

- Semester close AAR: count decisions logged, actions closed on time, reps completed. Those three numbers go in the last status report of the semester.
- AJ's lanes for Spring written and agreed with Chris. The succession conversation had, whatever its answer.
- Noah reps 3 and 4 done; his procedure page in the playbook.
- One page to Chris offering, for Spring: the typology cheat sheet for one sport administrator's care team, and one Grey Zone walkthrough with Athletic Medicine and Athletic Performance for one sport. Offered once, in writing.
- NCAA best-practices scope set as matrix plus procedures plus checklist.
- Intern module 1 rewritten as the Lab 1C submission.

## 9. Open questions only you can answer

1. Is AJ the successor, and will you say so to him and to Chris before December? Every "outlives" item depends on the answer.
2. Which ground is yours in the new structure: does Chris want you in the advisory-group and care-team conversations, or is Carrie the door and Chris the messenger?
3. Will you actually cut the education KR to two pieces on Oct 15 if there is no adoption signal, on the third cycle, knowing it will look like retreat?
4. The K-B placements: do you want them explicit and shared with AJ and Noah, as the course's workbook implies, or private? The course says cross-check with your boss. Is Chris that boss for this, given the review-authority question is still open?

5	## The model in one paragraph
6	
7	Four things have to exist for data to become decisions: people who can use the tools and want to (Phase 1), measurements you can repeat and interpret (Phase 2), forums where decisions are made, logged and reviewed (Phase 3), and pre-agreed pathways so a sound recommendation survives contact with the coach, the physician and the athlete's own case (Phase 4). The course's own summary of the failure mode is "tech-rich and procedure-poor" (module-1 note, Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.1). The course's summary of the fix is that discipline breeds freedom: standardised procedures produce reliability, reliability produces confidence, confidence produces decisions you can defend.
8	
9	## Phase 1. Foundation: common language and people
10	
11	**Objective.** Everyone in the interface (Applied Performance, Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine, coaches) can locate an athlete and a purpose in one sentence, and the leader knows who on staff can carry which responsibility.
12	
13	**Course tools.**
14	
15	- Means before modality before technology (module-1 note, Lab_1A_Blog pp.1-2).
16	- CM² athlete map, Control / Movement / Capacity / Maximum, or a local equivalent that is written down (module-1 note, Lab_1A_Blog pp.2-3).
17	- Knowledge-Behaviour Matrix and the Student Workbook sections A to D (module-1 note, Lab_1b_Blog pp.1-3; Knowledge_Behaviour_Profile_Student_Workbook pp.1-5).
18	- Leader-side probes: ask about CPD, ask for a ten-minute presentation on last month's work, test technical understanding (module-1 note, Lab 1B, transcript-only).
19	- "Five things that will derail this department" 60-second list (module-1 note, transcript-only).
20	- Translation audit: list every concept you re-explain to a second and third audience in the same week, then choose line-in-the-sand or education, and Option A (you teach) or Option B (empower the person who can) (module-4 note, Module_6B_Part_B pp.1-2).
21	- First-meeting operating statement when inheriting or resetting a group (module-4 note, Module_6B_Part_A p.2).
22	
23	**Steps.**
24	
25	1. The leader completes the Student Workbook first, privately: self-placement with evidence, three-to-five-year target, 30 to 90 day actions. Cross-check the self-placement with the supervisor.
26	2. Write the common language document. One page: the means/modality vocabulary, the athlete map with stage definitions, and each sport coach's verbal anchors for load and speed (jog, stride, sprint) so reports use the coach's words, not units (module-3 note, Webinar 3 Part II, transcript-only).
27	3. Map the staff in the interface on the matrix using role titles, with one observable behaviour per placement. Answer the four C2 questions: who is a handbrake with technology, who is a pawn with growth potential, who is an operator to learn from, who behaves like a catalyst.
28	4. Write one CPD plan per person from the matrix: the single axis they move on this semester, the reps that move it, the evidence that will show it moved.
29	5. Write the five derailers. Keep the list; re-read it at each semester checkpoint.
30	6. Run the translation audit. Every recurring re-explanation becomes either a line in the common language document or an education rep in Phase 3.
31	
32	**Artifacts.** Common language one-pager (distributed, in the onboarding pack). Private K-B map and CPD plans. Derailer list. Translation gap list.
33	
34	**Owner.** Director of Applied Performance drafts the language document and the audits. Director of Athletic Performance and the Senior Associate AD for Athlete Health endorse the language document so it carries across units. Each staff member owns their own workbook.
35	
36	**How you know it worked.** Staff use the stage words unprompted in a case conversation. "What are you trying to achieve with that drill?" replaces "why are you using that drill?" in a meeting. A coach asks a question in the anchor vocabulary. The number of times the leader re-explains the same concept in a week falls. Someone presents ten minutes on last month's work without being chased.
37	
38	## Phase 2. Technology and measurement discipline
39	
40	**Objective.** Every number that reaches a coach or a clinician can be repeated, has a known error band, and is attached to a question, an owner and a workflow.
41	
42	**Course tools.**
43	
44	- Tech Stack Reality Check: inventory by measurement system, raw signal vs reported metric, reliability evidence source, one-page procedure per tool (module-1 note, Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit pp.1-4).
45	- Measurement vs inference and the four-part report: measured, inferred, probability, next step (module-2 note, Lab_2a pp.1-4).
46	- Capability and Workflow Matrix: rows are technologies, columns are questions, each cell holds purpose, output, owner, workflow (module-2 note, Lab_2b pp.2-3).
47	- Monitoring vs testing procedure rule and the five coach questions (module-2 note, Lab_2c pp.1-2).
48	- Reliability vocabulary and decision logic: ICC, SEM/TE, MDC95, CV%, SWC (module-2 note, Lab_2E pp.1-2).
49	- Three failure modes: protocol drift, statistics-free interpretation, communication chaos (module-1 note, False_Promise pp.1-2).
50	- Six-stage decision pathway audit, especially the dirty-data and expertise-gap questions: who owns quality control, where were the thresholds inherited from, is there a handover when staff change (module-4 note, Lab 6D, transcript-only).
51	
52	**Steps.**
53	
54	1. Inventory by measurement system, not brand. Wearables, force plates, force transducers, linear position transducers, video, subjective measures, and the computer and software stack. One line each on raw signal, one on what is currently reported.
55	2. Fill the reliability column honestly: published, in-house repeat testing, or "we don't know yet". Expect most rows to say "we don't know yet". That column is the work list.
56	3. Write one one-page procedure at a time (warm-up, familiarisation, instructions, trial count, valid-rep and exclusion rules, reporting rule). Put it in the department playbook and the onboarding pack. Do not write all of them at once; write the one attached to a live decision.
57	4. Build the Capability and Workflow Matrix for the questions coaches actually ask. At least ten cells with purpose, output, owner (capture, understanding, upkeep) and workflow (capture, process, interpret, communicate, decide). List the gaps, bottlenecks and handoff risks the matrix exposes. Rule: if it is not in the matrix it is not in the workflow (module-2 note, transcript-only).
58	5. Label every metric in use as monitoring (status and trend, rolling baselines) or testing (progress, pre vs post). Tell coaches which is which before the season with the five questions. Never introduce a new variable mid-season (module-3 note, Webinar 3, transcript-only).
59	6. For the five metrics that feed decisions, establish in-house SEM/TE and MDC95, and CV% and SWC for the monitored ones, using your own equipment, testers and athletes. Treat early-phase force-time metrics (RFD) as noisy until proven otherwise; widen bands, tighten protocol or pick a more stable metric for gates (Lab_2E p.2).
60	7. Name the quality-control owner for each pipeline and write down what the check consists of. "Nobody, it's informal" is the finding.
61	8. Rewrite coach-facing reports in the four-part form and lead with the recommendation inside the first 20 seconds (module-4 note, Lab 6D, transcript-only).
62	
63	**Artifacts.** Inventory table with reliability column. Procedures in the playbook. Capability and Workflow Matrix with a gap list. Reliability table for the top five metrics. Pre-season coach cheat sheet in the coach's vocabulary. Named QC owner per pipeline.
64	
65	**Owner.** Director of Applied Performance owns the matrix, the reliability table and the QC assignments. Capture owners are whoever runs the device (Athletic Performance coach, athletic trainer, GA). Upkeep owner named per device.
66	
67	**How you know it worked.** A second person runs the test to the written procedure and gets a number inside the error band. A coach declines to react to a change that is inside MDC95, because the cheat sheet told them the error. A purchase or testing request arrives framed as a capacity question rather than a product name. The reliability column stops saying "we don't know yet", one row at a time. A report is read and acted on without the author in the room.
68	
69	## Phase 3. Meeting and communication operating rhythm
70	
71	**Objective.** Every standing forum has one named job, a time box, a pre-read and a logged output, and junior staff are getting leadership reps inside them.
72	
73	**Course tools.**
74	
75	- Four modalities (Decide, Diagnose, Inform, Build) plus the Learn application, and the five universal rules (module-3 note, Lab_3b_Meeting_Typology_Cheat_Sheet pp.1-2).
76	- Kaigi decision meeting prerequisites and agenda (module-3 note, Lab_3a_Blog pp.1-3).
77	- Pre-training go/no-go (module-3 note, Lab_3a_Blog p.2; run order transcript-only).
78	- Stoplight Storytelling one-slide brief with SEM and MDC95 on the slide, and the decision log with its CSV header (module-3 note, Lab_3c template pp.1-2).
79	- Lab 3D worksheet: meeting reps for staff with guardrails, success criteria, a four-rep ladder and a five-minute debrief (module-3 note, Lab_3D_Worksheet pp.1-3).
80	- Five operating practices: common language, communication mechanisms, operational procedures, strategic intent with scaled lanes, structured feedback (module-3 note, Webinar 3, transcript-only).
81	- Communication protocol per decision event: who is told, how fast, via which channel (module-4 note, The_Grey_Zone_Workbook p.7).
82	- Injury-communication tempo pre-agreed with the head coach (module-3 note, Webinar 3, transcript-only).
83	
84	**Steps.**
85	
86	1. Audit every standing invite the leader controls. Name the modality at the top, add the objective, duration and required prep. Where one meeting mixes modes, segment and time-box each segment and say so.
87	2. Start a decision log on the institution's shared surface (Teams, Planner or SharePoint, not a personal drive). Minimum fields: decision or ask as a verb, owner, action, due date, review date, notes with SEM/MDC where relevant. Athlete-level entries (gates, return-to-play calls) belong in the athlete management system, not the Teams log; the log records the department decision and points to the record. Rotate an "on audit" staff member to keep it as a development task (module-3 note, Lab 3A, transcript-only).
88	3. Pre-read 24 hours ahead for any Decide item; arrive informed or the meeting is catching up, not deciding.
89	4. Any ask that changes a plan (load, exposure, return-to-play progression) arrives as one stoplight slide: headline question, status, one chart, SEM and MDC95, one ask as a verb, owner, action, due, review. Amber must carry what is monitored and when it is reviewed.
90	5. Pick one junior staff member and one low-stakes forum (an ops stand-up) as rep one on the Lab 3D ladder. Set three non-negotiables, two allowed lane changes, the five success criteria, and the step-up threshold. Debrief for five minutes immediately after. Advance only on criteria met.
91	6. Agree the communication protocol table for the five decision events that touch field presence, with the head coach's notification path immediate and explicit.
92	7. Set a feedback cycle (monthly touch, semester review), document consequential conversations, and ask for feedback on yourself.
93	
94	**Artifacts.** Invite templates with modality, objective, duration, prep. Decision log on the shared surface. Stoplight slide template. One rep ladder per junior staff member. Communication protocol table. Pre-agreed injury-communication tempo per head coach.
95	
96	**Owner.** Director of Applied Performance for the forums Applied Performance runs. Director of Athletic Performance for the Athletic Performance staff meeting. Senior Associate AD for Athlete Health for the care-team and clinical forums. Sport administrators for sport care teams. The "on audit" role rotates among staff.
97	
98	**How you know it worked.** Meetings end on time. A later conversation cites the log ("we logged that on the 14th, review is Friday"). A junior staff member runs a forum without the leader present and the log entry is complete. Asks arrive as verbs. The leader's inbox shows fewer "can we catch up?" requests with no subject. The head coach hears about a field removal before the session ends, every time.
99	
100	## Phase 4. Integration and decision pathways
101	
102	**Objective.** A sound recommendation reaches a decision unchanged when its author is not in the room, and the clinical to training handoff runs on agreed rules rather than personality.
103	
104	**Course tools.**
105	
106	- Five integration breakpoints and the diagnostic questions (module-4 note, The_Leader_s_Integration_Cheat_Sheet p.1; The_Integration_Problem_Workbook pp.2, 4).
107	- Encoding realignment by scenario pre-commitment for one common presentation (module-4 note, Module_6B_Part_A p.1).
108	- Five-part decision gate: what is evaluated, pass/fail/borderline criteria, decision options, ownership, next step with time window (module-2 note, Lab_2D pp.1-2).
109	- Decision matrix: if this result, these steps, these owners, this re-check (module-2 note, Lab_2c p.2).
110	- Grey Zone build, seven steps: people profile, one operational logic, phase ownership map, cross-check, empowerment checklist, communication protocol, walkthrough, then the master checklist (module-4 note, The_Grey_Zone_Workbook pp.2-11).
111	- Triangulation plan and the six-check evidence stack: no single signal decides the outcome (module-2 note, Lab_2a p.3; Stacking_Evidence pp.2-4).
112	- Structured dissent: 10th Man in the decision log, pre-mortem review triggers, the four-layer Bias Prompt Analysis (module-4 note, Structured_Thinking_Under_Pressure pp.3-7).
113	
114	**Steps.**
115	
116	1. Run the three diagnostic questions on the department: when did our data last change a coaching decision; how many people can explain what the monitoring system measures; what happens to a recommendation when its author is absent. Trace one recent decision through the six stages and name the costliest breakpoint.
117	2. Profile the people in the clinical to training interface on the matrix (Grey Zone step 1) before designing anything. The same protocol works with one pairing and fails with another.
118	3. Facilitate the One Operational Logic table: agreed positions on rehab markers, running readiness, return-to-training threshold, data trusted in-house, data never acted on alone, what "ready" means. A blank row is the priority.
119	4. Write the Rehab Phase Ownership Map. In the university model the team physician holds legal clearance, so Athletic Medicine owns the clearance gates at Return to Function and Return to Competition regardless of who owns operational progression in between; Athletic Performance owns Return to Run in most cases; Return to Play is shared on pre-agreed criteria.
120	5. Fill the seven-row Decision Empowerment Checklist and the five-event Communication Protocol for one sport first.
121	6. Write two decision gates, one performance (speed or deceleration exposure) and one rehab (hamstring return to run), with criteria in local MDC and SWC units and timeframes inside the gate.
122	7. Pre-commit one common presentation (for example a grade 2 hamstring): assessment, checkpoints, day-by-day tempo, realistic timeline, who acts at each handover, criteria for deviating. This document is what the coach sees.
123	8. Run the Walkthrough Exercise once per semester or after any staff change: one case told twice, clinical eyes then training eyes, mark divergence points, write the integration protocol for the top one.
124	9. Put the Evidence Stack Card in the case-review agenda and a named 10th Man in the log before any return-to-play or programme decision is recorded, with the top two pre-mortem answers stored as review triggers.
125	
126	**Artifacts.** Breakpoint diagnosis for one real case. Grey Zone workbook filled for one sport. Two written gates. One scenario pre-commitment document. Evidence Stack Card in the case-review template. Walkthrough record with integration protocols.
127	
128	**Owner.** Senior Associate AD for Athlete Health sponsors the grey-zone work and the advisory forum where it is reviewed. Athletic Medicine lead owns clearance gates. Athletic Performance lead owns return-to-run progression. Director of Applied Performance owns the data columns, the reliability under every gate, and facilitation of the walkthrough.
129	
130	**How you know it worked.** The cross-check passes: the athletic trainer can state what the performance coach will do next week and vice versa (module-4 note, Video_Lab_The_Grey_Zone_Summary p.4). A gate outcome is referenced later rather than re-argued. A recommendation holds when its author is absent. An override is recorded with a reason instead of happening silently. A 10th Man argument appears in the log and changes a contingency at least once a semester.
131	
132	## What must survive the leader leaving
133	
134	The course draws the line between the operating system, which travels and survives, and what the leader personally carries. "Build it once and sell it fifteen times" is the speaker's phrase for procedures (module-3 note, Webinar 3 Part III, transcript-only); "if it is not in the workflow it does not exist" is the test (module-2 note, transcript-only).
135	
136	| Operating system (must be installed) | Where it must live | Non-leader owner |
137	| --- | --- | --- |
138	| Common language one-pager and coach cheat sheets | Onboarding pack, shared drive of the unit, not a personal folder | Director of Athletic Performance endorses; each sport's Applied Performance contact maintains |
139	| One-page procedures per tool | Department playbook | Capture owner per device |
140	| Capability and Workflow Matrix with owners | Shared surface, reviewed each semester | Rotating "on audit" staff member updates |
141	| Reliability table (SEM, MDC95, SWC) | Same file as the matrix | Whoever owns understanding for the device |
142	| Invite templates with modality, objective, duration, prep | Outlook templates, Teams channel description | Any staff member who runs a forum |
143	| Decision log | Teams or Planner, institutional tenancy | Rotating "on audit" role |
144	| Decision Empowerment Checklist and Communication Protocol | Playbook SOP, signed by the sponsoring AD | Athletic Medicine lead and Athletic Performance lead jointly |
145	| Written decision gates and scenario pre-commitments | Athlete management system or playbook | Athletic Medicine lead |
146	| Lab 3D rep ladder and success criteria | Playbook staff-development section | Whoever supervises the junior staff member |
147	
148	What the leader personally carries and cannot fully hand over: relationships with coaches and administrators, judgment on contested metrics, the coalition that gets a sponsor to sign. The course's answer is to encode as much as possible in advance: scenario pre-commitment converts judgment into a document; Option B (empower the person who can teach the framework) converts a personal skill into a role; scaling lanes up for a successor before the leader leaves converts trust into written decision rights. The handover test is the six-stage pathway's expertise-gap question: is there a high-clarity handover when staff change, with thresholds, their origin and their reviewer written down?
149	
150	Two rules make this real. First, nothing counts as installed while it lives only on the leader's laptop, personal cloud or private notes. Second, every artifact in the table above has a named owner who is not the leader by the end of the first year, even if the leader still does most of the work.
151	
152	## Sequencing rationale
153	
154	- People before process. The Grey Zone Workbook says profile the pairing before designing the protocol, because the same model succeeds with one pair and fails with another (module-4 note, Grey Zone Summary p.2). That is why Phase 1 is first and the matrix is its centre.
155	- Means before technology. Lab 1A's ordering and Lab 2C's "we have force plates, so we should jump" warning both say the question comes before the device (Lab_2c p.2). Phase 2 therefore starts with inventory and the question list, not with buying or building.
156	- Reliability before gates. A gate with criteria in units nobody has measured the error of is a meeting, not a decision (Lab_2D p.2; Lab_2E p.1). Phase 4's gates depend on Phase 2's reliability table.
157	- Meetings are the delivery mechanism. Common language, thresholds and assigned actions get enforced in forums, so Phase 3 can start on day one for the forums the leader controls and should run in parallel with Phase 2. It needs no sponsor.
158	- Integration last because it needs a sponsor. Phase 4 touches clinical authority and coach communication; it is offered to the people who own those lanes, and it is cheap to offer only once Phases 1 to 3 have produced the language, the numbers and the log it runs on.
159	- Small steps. Every phase is written so its first artifact is one page and its first rep is one meeting. The course is explicit that confidence follows repetition, not the reverse (Lab_3D_Blog p.2).
160	
161	## Dependency map
162	
163	| Item | Depends on | Enables |
164	| --- | --- | --- |
165	| Leader self-audit (P1) | Nothing | Staff K-B map, CPD plans |
166	| Common language one-pager (P1) | Leader self-audit | Coach cheat sheet, stoplight slides, care-team vocabulary |
167	| Staff K-B map and CPD plans (P1) | Leader self-audit | Rep ladders (P3), grey-zone people profile (P4), lane scaling |
168	| Tech inventory with reliability column (P2) | Nothing | Procedures, matrix, reliability table |
169	| One-page procedures (P2) | Inventory | Onboarding pack, repeatable numbers, QC owner |
170	| Capability and Workflow Matrix (P2) | Inventory, common language | Gap list, monitoring vs testing labels, HPI-type integration work |
171	| Reliability table (P2) | Procedures, in-house repeat testing | Stoplight slides, decision gates, coach cheat sheet error bands |
172	| Invite audit and decision log (P3) | Nothing | Everything downstream that needs a logged decision |
173	| Stoplight slide in use (P3) | Reliability table for the metric shown | Kaigi throughput, status-report decisions |
174	| Rep ladder for junior staff (P3) | K-B map, a low-stakes forum | Succession, "on audit" role |
175	| Communication protocol (P3/P4) | Sponsor agreement | Field-removal notification, escalation without surprise |
176	| Grey Zone workbook for one sport (P4) | People profile, common language, sponsor | Empowerment checklist, ownership map, walkthrough |
177	| Decision gates (P4) | Reliability table, ownership map | Return-to-play decisions that hold when the author is absent |
178	| Structured dissent in the log (P4) | Decision log | Groupthink counterweight once aligned |

- CM² athlete map, Control / Movement / Capacity / Maximum, or a local equivalent that is written down (module-1 note, Lab_1A_Blog pp.2-3).
- Knowledge-Behaviour Matrix and the Student Workbook sections A to D (module-1 note, Lab_1b_Blog pp.1-3; Knowledge_Behaviour_Profile_Student_Workbook pp.1-5).
- Leader-side probes: ask about CPD, ask for a ten-minute presentation on last month's work, test technical understanding (module-1 note, Lab 1B, transcript-only).
- "Five things that will derail this department" 60-second list (module-1 note, transcript-only).
- Translation audit: list every concept you re-explain to a second and third audience in the same week, then choose line-in-the-sand or education, and Option A (you teach) or Option B (empower the person who can) (module-4 note, Module_6B_Part_B pp.1-2).
- First-meeting operating statement when inheriting or resetting a group (module-4 note, Module_6B_Part_A p.2).

**Steps.**

1. The leader completes the Student Workbook first, privately: self-placement with evidence, three-to-five-year target, 30 to 90 day actions. Cross-check the self-placement with the supervisor.
2. Write the common language document. One page: the means/modality vocabulary, the athlete map with stage definitions, and each sport coach's verbal anchors for load and speed (jog, stride, sprint) so reports use the coach's words, not units (module-3 note, Webinar 3 Part II, transcript-only).
3. Map the staff in the interface on the matrix using role titles, with one observable behaviour per placement. Answer the four C2 questions: who is a handbrake with technology, who is a pawn with growth potential, who is an operator to learn from, who behaves like a catalyst.
4. Write one CPD plan per person from the matrix: the single axis they move on this semester, the reps that move it, the evidence that will show it moved.
5. Write the five derailers. Keep the list; re-read it at each semester checkpoint.
6. Run the translation audit. Every recurring re-explanation becomes either a line in the common language document or an education rep in Phase 3.

**Artifacts.** Common language one-pager (distributed, in the onboarding pack). Private K-B map and CPD plans. Derailer list. Translation gap list.

**Owner.** Director of Applied Performance drafts the language document and the audits. Director of Athletic Performance and the Senior Associate AD for Athlete Health endorse the language document so it carries across units. Each staff member owns their own workbook.

**How you know it worked.** Staff use the stage words unprompted in a case conversation. "What are you trying to achieve with that drill?" replaces "why are you using that drill?" in a meeting. A coach asks a question in the anchor vocabulary. The number of times the leader re-explains the same concept in a week falls. Someone presents ten minutes on last month's work without being chased.

## Phase 2. Technology and measurement discipline

**Objective.** Every number that reaches a coach or a clinician can be repeated, has a known error band, and is attached to a question, an owner and a workflow.

**Course tools.**

- Tech Stack Reality Check: inventory by measurement system, raw signal vs reported metric, reliability evidence source, one-page procedure per tool (module-1 note, Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit pp.1-4).
- Measurement vs inference and the four-part report: measured, inferred, probability, next step (module-2 note, Lab_2a pp.1-4).
- Capability and Workflow Matrix: rows are technologies, columns are questions, each cell holds purpose, output, owner, workflow (module-2 note, Lab_2b pp.2-3).
- Monitoring vs testing procedure rule and the five coach questions (module-2 note, Lab_2c pp.1-2).
- Reliability vocabulary and decision logic: ICC, SEM/TE, MDC95, CV%, SWC (module-2 note, Lab_2E pp.1-2).
- Three failure modes: protocol drift, statistics-free interpretation, communication chaos (module-1 note, False_Promise pp.1-2).
- Six-stage decision pathway audit, especially the dirty-data and expertise-gap questions: who owns quality control, where were the thresholds inherited from, is there a handover when staff change (module-4 note, Lab 6D, transcript-only).

**Steps.**

1. Inventory by measurement system, not brand. Wearables, force plates, force transducers, linear position transducers, video, subjective measures, and the computer and software stack. One line each on raw signal, one on what is currently reported.
2. Fill the reliability column honestly: published, in-house repeat testing, or "we don't know yet". Expect most rows to say "we don't know yet". That column is the work list.
3. Write one one-page procedure at a time (warm-up, familiarisation, instructions, trial count, valid-rep and exclusion rules, reporting rule). Put it in the department playbook and the onboarding pack. Do not write all of them at once; write the one attached to a live decision.
4. Build the Capability and Workflow Matrix for the questions coaches actually ask. At least ten cells with purpose, output, owner (capture, understanding, upkeep) and workflow (capture, process, interpret, communicate, decide). List the gaps, bottlenecks and handoff risks the matrix exposes. Rule: if it is not in the matrix it is not in the workflow (module-2 note, transcript-only).
5. Label every metric in use as monitoring (status and trend, rolling baselines) or testing (progress, pre vs post). Tell coaches which is which before the season with the five questions. Never introduce a new variable mid-season (module-3 note, Webinar 3, transcript-only).
6. For the five metrics that feed decisions, establish in-house SEM/TE and MDC95, and CV% and SWC for the monitored ones, using your own equipment, testers and athletes. Treat early-phase force-time metrics (RFD) as noisy until proven otherwise; widen bands, tighten protocol or pick a more stable metric for gates (Lab_2E p.2).
7. Name the quality-control owner for each pipeline and write down what the check consists of. "Nobody, it's informal" is the finding.
8. Rewrite coach-facing reports in the four-part form and lead with the recommendation inside the first 20 seconds (module-4 note, Lab 6D, transcript-only).

**Artifacts.** Inventory table with reliability column. Procedures in the playbook. Capability and Workflow Matrix with a gap list. Reliability table for the top five metrics. Pre-season coach cheat sheet in the coach's vocabulary. Named QC owner per pipeline.

**Owner.** Director of Applied Performance owns the matrix, the reliability table and the QC assignments. Capture owners are whoever runs the device (Athletic Performance coach, athletic trainer, GA). Upkeep owner named per device.

**How you know it worked.** A second person runs the test to the written procedure and gets a number inside the error band. A coach declines to react to a change that is inside MDC95, because the cheat sheet told them the error. A purchase or testing request arrives framed as a capacity question rather than a product name. The reliability column stops saying "we don't know yet", one row at a time. A report is read and acted on without the author in the room.

## Phase 3. Meeting and communication operating rhythm

**Objective.** Every standing forum has one named job, a time box, a pre-read and a logged output, and junior staff are getting leadership reps inside them.

**Course tools.**

- Four modalities (Decide, Diagnose, Inform, Build) plus the Learn application, and the five universal rules (module-3 note, Lab_3b_Meeting_Typology_Cheat_Sheet pp.1-2).
- Kaigi decision meeting prerequisites and agenda (module-3 note, Lab_3a_Blog pp.1-3).
- Pre-training go/no-go (module-3 note, Lab_3a_Blog p.2; run order transcript-only).
- Stoplight Storytelling one-slide brief with SEM and MDC95 on the slide, and the decision log with its CSV header (module-3 note, Lab_3c template pp.1-2).
- Lab 3D worksheet: meeting reps for staff with guardrails, success criteria, a four-rep ladder and a five-minute debrief (module-3 note, Lab_3D_Worksheet pp.1-3).
- Five operating practices: common language, communication mechanisms, operational procedures, strategic intent with scaled lanes, structured feedback (module-3 note, Webinar 3, transcript-only).
- Communication protocol per decision event: who is told, how fast, via which channel (module-4 note, The_Grey_Zone_Workbook p.7).
- Injury-communication tempo pre-agreed with the head coach (module-3 note, Webinar 3, transcript-only).

**Steps.**

1. Audit every standing invite the leader controls. Name the modality at the top, add the objective, duration and required prep. Where one meeting mixes modes, segment and time-box each segment and say so.
2. Start a decision log on the institution's shared surface (Teams, Planner or SharePoint, not a personal drive). Minimum fields: decision or ask as a verb, owner, action, due date, review date, notes with SEM/MDC where relevant. Athlete-level entries (gates, return-to-play calls) belong in the athlete management system, not the Teams log; the log records the department decision and points to the record. Rotate an "on audit" staff member to keep it as a development task (module-3 note, Lab 3A, transcript-only).
3. Pre-read 24 hours ahead for any Decide item; arrive informed or the meeting is catching up, not deciding.
4. Any ask that changes a plan (load, exposure, return-to-play progression) arrives as one stoplight slide: headline question, status, one chart, SEM and MDC95, one ask as a verb, owner, action, due, review. Amber must carry what is monitored and when it is reviewed.
5. Pick one junior staff member and one low-stakes forum (an ops stand-up) as rep one on the Lab 3D ladder. Set three non-negotiables, two allowed lane changes, the five success criteria, and the step-up threshold. Debrief for five minutes immediately after. Advance only on criteria met.
6. Agree the communication protocol table for the five decision events that touch field presence, with the head coach's notification path immediate and explicit.
7. Set a feedback cycle (monthly touch, semester review), document consequential conversations, and ask for feedback on yourself.

**Artifacts.** Invite templates with modality, objective, duration, prep. Decision log on the shared surface. Stoplight slide template. One rep ladder per junior staff member. Communication protocol table. Pre-agreed injury-communication tempo per head coach.

**Owner.** Director of Applied Performance for the forums Applied Performance runs. Director of Athletic Performance for the Athletic Performance staff meeting. Senior Associate AD for Athlete Health for the care-team and clinical forums. Sport administrators for sport care teams. The "on audit" role rotates among staff.

**How you know it worked.** Meetings end on time. A later conversation cites the log ("we logged that on the 14th, review is Friday"). A junior staff member runs a forum without the leader present and the log entry is complete. Asks arrive as verbs. The leader's inbox shows fewer "can we catch up?" requests with no subject. The head coach hears about a field removal before the session ends, every time.

## Phase 4. Integration and decision pathways

**Objective.** A sound recommendation reaches a decision unchanged when its author is not in the room, and the clinical to training handoff runs on agreed rules rather than personality.

**Course tools.**

- Five integration breakpoints and the diagnostic questions (module-4 note, The_Leader_s_Integration_Cheat_Sheet p.1; The_Integration_Problem_Workbook pp.2, 4).
- Encoding realignment by scenario pre-commitment for one common presentation (module-4 note, Module_6B_Part_A p.1).
- Five-part decision gate: what is evaluated, pass/fail/borderline criteria, decision options, ownership, next step with time window (module-2 note, Lab_2D pp.1-2).
- Decision matrix: if this result, these steps, these owners, this re-check (module-2 note, Lab_2c p.2).
- Grey Zone build, seven steps: people profile, one operational logic, phase ownership map, cross-check, empowerment checklist, communication protocol, walkthrough, then the master checklist (module-4 note, The_Grey_Zone_Workbook pp.2-11).
- Triangulation plan and the six-check evidence stack: no single signal decides the outcome (module-2 note, Lab_2a p.3; Stacking_Evidence pp.2-4).
- Structured dissent: 10th Man in the decision log, pre-mortem review triggers, the four-layer Bias Prompt Analysis (module-4 note, Structured_Thinking_Under_Pressure pp.3-7).

**Steps.**

1. Run the three diagnostic questions on the department: when did our data last change a coaching decision; how many people can explain what the monitoring system measures; what happens to a recommendation when its author is absent. Trace one recent decision through the six stages and name the costliest breakpoint.
2. Profile the people in the clinical to training interface on the matrix (Grey Zone step 1) before designing anything. The same protocol works with one pairing and fails with another.
3. Facilitate the One Operational Logic table: agreed positions on rehab markers, running readiness, return-to-training threshold, data trusted in-house, data never acted on alone, what "ready" means. A blank row is the priority.
4. Write the Rehab Phase Ownership Map. In the university model the team physician holds legal clearance, so Athletic Medicine owns the clearance gates at Return to Function and Return to Competition regardless of who owns operational progression in between; Athletic Performance owns Return to Run in most cases; Return to Play is shared on pre-agreed criteria.
5. Fill the seven-row Decision Empowerment Checklist and the five-event Communication Protocol for one sport first.
6. Write two decision gates, one performance (speed or deceleration exposure) and one rehab (hamstring return to run), with criteria in local MDC and SWC units and timeframes inside the gate.
7. Pre-commit one common presentation (for example a grade 2 hamstring): assessment, checkpoints, day-by-day tempo, realistic timeline, who acts at each handover, criteria for deviating. This document is what the coach sees.
8. Run the Walkthrough Exercise once per semester or after any staff change: one case told twice, clinical eyes then training eyes, mark divergence points, write the integration protocol for the top one.
9. Put the Evidence Stack Card in the case-review agenda and a named 10th Man in the log before any return-to-play or programme decision is recorded, with the top two pre-mortem answers stored as review triggers.

**Artifacts.** Breakpoint diagnosis for one real case. Grey Zone workbook filled for one sport. Two written gates. One scenario pre-commitment document. Evidence Stack Card in the case-review template. Walkthrough record with integration protocols.

**Owner.** Senior Associate AD for Athlete Health sponsors the grey-zone work and the advisory forum where it is reviewed. Athletic Medicine lead owns clearance gates. Athletic Performance lead owns return-to-run progression. Director of Applied Performance owns the data columns, the reliability under every gate, and facilitation of the walkthrough.

**How you know it worked.** The cross-check passes: the athletic trainer can state what the performance coach will do next week and vice versa (module-4 note, Video_Lab_The_Grey_Zone_Summary p.4). A gate outcome is referenced later rather than re-argued. A recommendation holds when its author is absent. An override is recorded with a reason instead of happening silently. A 10th Man argument appears in the log and changes a contingency at least once a semester.

## What must survive the leader leaving

The course draws the line between the operating system, which travels and survives, and what the leader personally carries. "Build it once and sell it fifteen times" is the speaker's phrase for procedures (module-3 note, Webinar 3 Part III, transcript-only); "if it is not in the workflow it does not exist" is the test (module-2 note, transcript-only).

| Operating system (must be installed) | Where it must live | Non-leader owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Common language one-pager and coach cheat sheets | Onboarding pack, shared drive of the unit, not a personal folder | Director of Athletic Performance endorses; each sport's Applied Performance contact maintains |
| One-page procedures per tool | Department playbook | Capture owner per device |
| Capability and Workflow Matrix with owners | Shared surface, reviewed each semester | Rotating "on audit" staff member updates |
| Reliability table (SEM, MDC95, SWC) | Same file as the matrix | Whoever owns understanding for the device |
| Invite templates with modality, objective, duration, prep | Outlook templates, Teams channel description | Any staff member who runs a forum |
| Decision log | Teams or Planner, institutional tenancy | Rotating "on audit" role |
| Decision Empowerment Checklist and Communication Protocol | Playbook SOP, signed by the sponsoring AD | Athletic Medicine lead and Athletic Performance lead jointly |
| Written decision gates and scenario pre-commitments | Athlete management system or playbook | Athletic Medicine lead |
| Lab 3D rep ladder and success criteria | Playbook staff-development section | Whoever supervises the junior staff member |

What the leader personally carries and cannot fully hand over: relationships with coaches and administrators, judgment on contested metrics, the coalition that gets a sponsor to sign. The course's answer is to encode as much as possible in advance: scenario pre-commitment converts judgment into a document; Option B (empower the person who can teach the framework) converts a personal skill into a role; scaling lanes up for a successor before the leader leaves converts trust into written decision rights. The handover test is the six-stage pathway's expertise-gap question: is there a high-clarity handover when staff change, with thresholds, their origin and their reviewer written down?

Two rules make this real. First, nothing counts as installed while it lives only on the leader's laptop, personal cloud or private notes. Second, every artifact in the table above has a named owner who is not the leader by the end of the first year, even if the leader still does most of the work.

## Sequencing rationale

- People before process. The Grey Zone Workbook says profile the pairing before designing the protocol, because the same model succeeds with one pair and fails with another (module-4 note, Grey Zone Summary p.2). That is why Phase 1 is first and the matrix is its centre.
- Means before technology. Lab 1A's ordering and Lab 2C's "we have force plates, so we should jump" warning both say the question comes before the device (Lab_2c p.2). Phase 2 therefore starts with inventory and the question list, not with buying or building.
- Reliability before gates. A gate with criteria in units nobody has measured the error of is a meeting, not a decision (Lab_2D p.2; Lab_2E p.1). Phase 4's gates depend on Phase 2's reliability table.
- Meetings are the delivery mechanism. Common language, thresholds and assigned actions get enforced in forums, so Phase 3 can start on day one for the forums the leader controls and should run in parallel with Phase 2. It needs no sponsor.
- Integration last because it needs a sponsor. Phase 4 touches clinical authority and coach communication; it is offered to the people who own those lanes, and it is cheap to offer only once Phases 1 to 3 have produced the language, the numbers and the log it runs on.
- Small steps. Every phase is written so its first artifact is one page and its first rep is one meeting. The course is explicit that confidence follows repetition, not the reverse (Lab_3D_Blog p.2).

## Dependency map

| Item | Depends on | Enables |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Leader self-audit (P1) | Nothing | Staff K-B map, CPD plans |
| Common language one-pager (P1) | Leader self-audit | Coach cheat sheet, stoplight slides, care-team vocabulary |
| Staff K-B map and CPD plans (P1) | Leader self-audit | Rep ladders (P3), grey-zone people profile (P4), lane scaling |
| Tech inventory with reliability column (P2) | Nothing | Procedures, matrix, reliability table |
| One-page procedures (P2) | Inventory | Onboarding pack, repeatable numbers, QC owner |
| Capability and Workflow Matrix (P2) | Inventory, common language | Gap list, monitoring vs testing labels, HPI-type integration work |
| Reliability table (P2) | Procedures, in-house repeat testing | Stoplight slides, decision gates, coach cheat sheet error bands |
| Invite audit and decision log (P3) | Nothing | Everything downstream that needs a logged decision |
| Stoplight slide in use (P3) | Reliability table for the metric shown | Kaigi throughput, status-report decisions |
| Rep ladder for junior staff (P3) | K-B map, a low-stakes forum | Succession, "on audit" role |
| Communication protocol (P3/P4) | Sponsor agreement | Field-removal notification, escalation without surprise |
| Grey Zone workbook for one sport (P4) | People profile, common language, sponsor | Empowerment checklist, ownership map, walkthrough |
| Decision gates (P4) | Reliability table, ownership map | Return-to-play decisions that hold when the author is absent |
| Structured dissent in the log (P4) | Decision log | Groupthink counterweight once aligned |

1	# Eric Rash context brief (for staff-development and department-building recommendations)
2	
3	Compiled 2026-09-24 from the DEV workspace, the SecondBrain vault, and Claude memory. Read-only pass; nothing else was modified. Sources are date-stamped in section 8 because they span June to September 2026 and some are stale. Anything not stated in a source is marked (inferred). No athlete names or athlete health information appear here by design.
4	
5	Naming rule for anything staff-facing that comes out of this: Athletic Performance (not S&C), Athletic Medicine (not sports medicine), Applied Performance (not sport science).
6	
7	## Role and remit
8	
9	- Title: Director of Applied Performance, Baylor University Athletics. About eight years in the department, promoted into the director seat from within. Source: `ContextVault/Career-Context-Document.md` (2026-06-08).
10	- Where the unit sits: Applied Performance is a support and enablement function inside Health & Wellness, behind the athlete-facing units (Athletic Medicine, Athletic Performance, Mental Health, Performance Nutrition). It is not athlete-facing itself. Source: Career-Context-Document; `Education_Alignment_Initiative/docs/context.md`.
11	- Reporting line: formal supervisor is Chris Ruf, Director of Athletic Performance, since a 2025 reporting change that moved Eric off administrative senior staff (where he reported to Kenny Boyd, Executive Senior Associate AD). The June career document records that the change cost him access to Kenny and senior conversations. Since then: the July 2026 responsibilities document came from Chris and Kenny jointly, the biweekly status report goes to both, and in August Kenny named Eric the Athletics point of contact to ITS. Some access to Kenny has been rebuilt through the JD process and the technology work (inferred). Chris prefers email. Sources: Career-Context-Document; `KeystoneOS memory project-jd-okr-2026.md`; `SoftwareTech_Mgmt_Framework/docs/MICAH_MEETING_REQUEST_2026-08-13.md`; `BAIR_Steering_Committee/docs/context.md` (which lists Kenny as the person Eric reports to; treat as the BAIR-lane relationship, not the formal line).
12	- The July 2026 JD shifted the role from doer to director. It names: department oversight, BAIR Steering Committee oversight and organization, HPI (human performance integration) protocols, technology vetting, vendor relations and onboarding, data infrastructure, guidance to Health & Wellness staff on technology and data, and Spirit Squad as a direct team-training responsibility. Source: `project-jd-okr-2026.md`; `SecondBrain/Projects/Applied-Performance-JD-2026/decisions.md` (2026-07-17).
13	- Three permanent service pillars in the current OKR structure (v3): Data Systems & Analytics, Education, Research & Development, plus an enabling objective, Leadership & Visibility. Mission sentence used in briefings: "Applied Performance turns Baylor's athlete data into decisions that keep athletes available and performing." North star: be the best applied performance department in the country. Source: `SecondBrain/Projects/Applied-Performance-OKRs-2026-27.md` (v3, Fall set authored 2026-09-14).
14	- Eric's protected hands-on lanes (not delegated): HPI protocol and its dashboarding; technology vetting; white-paper analysis; one-off reports and dashboards for sports. Delegation stops at those boundaries. Source: OKR doc v3.
15	- Decision rights (June 2026 read): owns what projects to pursue, what questions to chase, how to source data, and can take a meeting with almost anyone on campus. Needs Chris for spending and hiring. No budget line. No control over whether other units adopt his work. The JD clarifying questions (July) show that authority thresholds, budget, evaluation of staff, and escalation were still undefined at that point. Sources: Career-Context-Document; `SecondBrain/Projects/Applied-Performance-JD-2026/JD-clarifying-questions.md`.
16	- Accountability: Eric authors his own OKRs; no one external holds him to them. The v3 system adds self-imposed teeth: semester cycles, an Oct 15 mid-semester checkpoint, a Dec 18 close, and a timer-checked project slate. Source: OKR doc v3; `SecondBrain/Projects/Applied-Performance-Operating-Cadence.md` (2026-09-14).
17	
18	## Staff and structure
19	
20	Applied Performance unit (as of the v3 OKR doc and the 2026-08-24 supervisor update):
21	
22	- Eric Rash, Director. Presents solo in briefings; staff appear on the org and lanes slide.
